feed.subtitle: Huong (Christine) Van Le. Applied machine learning researcher working on AI for drug discovery, ADMET prediction, and structure-based design.

entry.title: Coverage is not a property of a dataset

link.title: Coverage is not a property of a dataset

entry.content:
Most of the time, a model’s relationship to its training data is treated as a filter. A prediction comes out, you ask whether the query compound falls inside the applicability domain, and if it does not you discount the number. That is a defensive question, and a useful one.

Lately I have been thinking about the same relationship from the other side. Suppose you are not only consuming a dataset but able to add to it — you can ask a laboratory to measure a handful of new compounds, and you have to say which ones. The defensive question becomes a design question: not is this prediction trustworthy, but what is this dataset missing, and what should we measure next.

It sounds like a straightforward thing to work out. Project the dataset into some space, look for the empty regions, go and fill them. The more I look at it, the less straightforward it gets, and the reason is that the word “missing” does not survive contact with a definition.

Datasets have the shape of the projects that produced them

Public ADMET data is not a sample of chemical space. It is an accumulation of whatever a few hundred medicinal chemistry programmes happened to make, measured by whichever laboratories happened to publish. Compounds arrive in series: a scaffold, then thirty variations on it, because that is how optimisation campaigns work. Whole regions are dense because a target was fashionable in 2009, and whole regions are empty because nobody had a reason to go there.

A model trained on that inherits the shape. It will be confident in the neighbourhoods where the data piled up and uninformative everywhere else, and the boundary between the two has nothing to do with where chemistry is interesting. So the instinct to go and fill the empty parts is sound. The difficulty is saying which parts those are.

Empty relative to what?

The first problem is that a hole needs a reference. A dataset is not empty in the abstract; it is empty relative to some universe you think it ought to cover.

Pick ChEMBL as the universe and your gaps are wherever bioactive chemistry has been explored but your assay has not followed. Pick a purchasable catalogue and the gaps move to wherever compounds are cheaply available and untested — a much more actionable set, and a much more commercially biased one, because catalogues reflect what is easy to make. Pick the chemotypes around one target family and you get a third answer again, narrower and more useful for one programme and useless for the next.

These are not refinements of a single question. They are three different questions that produce three different shopping lists, and the choice between them is made before any analysis happens. I have read a reasonable amount of work in this area and the reference set is very often left implicit.

Empty in which space?

The second problem is sharper, and it is the one I keep coming back to, because I ran into the evidence for it in my own published work.

Emptiness is a statement about density, and density requires a metric. Write $\phi$ for whatever featurisation turns a molecule into a vector. It induces a distance

\[d_\phi(x, y) = \lVert \phi(x) - \phi(y) \rVert\]

and a hole is a region where the density of the dataset under $d_\phi$ is low while its surroundings are not. Nothing in that definition is a property of the molecules alone. Change $\phi$ and you change which compounds count as neighbours, which changes where the density is low, which changes what is missing.

That is not a theoretical worry. In CaliciBoost we compared eight molecular representations on one permeability task through a single fixed pipeline, and they did not agree — not on performance, and by implication not on which compounds resemble which. If eight featurisations disagree about similarity, they disagree about holes.

Here is the effect on a library I enumerated to look at it directly. Same molecules, two standard featurisations, each reduced to two dimensions and binned on the same grid; a hatched cell is an empty region fully enclosed by occupied ones.

The two panels are the same compounds. One space says this library is full of holes; the other says it is essentially solid. And the compounds that sit on the rim of a gap in the first space — the ones you would reach for if you were trying to fill it — are scattered across the second, bordering nothing.

I want to be careful not to overstate what a figure like this shows. It is an enumerated library, not a real assay set, and two dimensions of PCA is a crude view of either space. But the direction of the effect is not an artefact of those choices, and it is enough to make the point that interests me: a gap is a property of a dataset and a featurisation together, and the featurisation is a modelling decision somebody made. Two groups can analyse the same dataset, both honestly conclude that it has holes, and commission entirely different experiments.

You cannot order a point in chemical space

There is a third difficulty, and it is the one I suspect is least appreciated in the machine learning literature, because it does not arise in the settings where that literature was developed.

Active learning assumes a pool. You identify the most informative point and you query its label. In a laboratory you cannot do that. What you identify is a location — a position $z$ in feature space where data would help — and what you can actually buy or make is whatever the catalogue happens to contain:

\[x^\star = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x \,\in\, \mathcal{C}} \; d_\phi\big(\phi(x),\, z\big)\]

That residual distance is the gap between what you wanted and what you can get, and it is not small. It is also, inevitably, measured in the same $\phi$ whose arbitrariness is the problem in the first place. Add that synthesis cost is wildly uneven across regions — the empty parts of chemical space are sometimes empty precisely because they are hard to make — and the clean picture of filling a void starts to look like a constrained optimisation with an objective nobody has written down carefully.

And then, how would you know it worked

Suppose you do it anyway: define a space, define a universe, pick compounds, run the assays, retrain. How do you tell whether it helped?

The tempting answer is to report the change in global test error, and I think that is the wrong statistic — for the same reason I argued about multitask models recently. If you added fifty compounds in one sparse region of a thousand-compound set, the global mean is mostly noise from everywhere else. What you want to know is whether the model improved in the region you filled, and whether it did so more than the same budget spent at random or on the points the model was least certain about. Those baselines are not optional. Coverage-driven selection is one of several established strategies, and the literature on uncertainty sampling, query-by-committee and core-set selection is old enough that a new method has to beat them rather than cite them.

Where this leaves me

I am working on this, and I have nothing to report yet — no method I am ready to defend and no numbers. What I have is a reframing that I think is correct and that I have not seen stated plainly:

Coverage is not a property of a dataset. It is a property of a dataset, a featurisation, and a reference universe — and most of the time only the first is reported.

If that is right, then “we identified gaps in chemical space and designed experiments to fill them” is an incomplete sentence, and two papers making that claim may not be comparable at all. Whether the choice of featurisation changes the outcome of a gap-filling campaign, and not merely its shopping list, is an empirical question. It is the one I would most like to answer, and it is answerable retrospectively, before anyone spends money at the bench.

That seems like the right order to do it in.
entry.summary: On what it means for a chemical dataset to have a hole in it, and why the answer depends on who is asking

entry.title: Multitask ADMET models, and what the average improvement hides

link.title: Multitask ADMET models, and what the average improvement hides

entry.content:
Training one model to predict many ADMET endpoints is an appealing idea, and the argument for it is sound. Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity all depend on overlapping structural features — size, lipophilicity, polarity, the presence of particular functional groups. A single encoder that learns those features once, feeding a separate head per endpoint, should let an endpoint with four hundred measurements borrow representation from one with forty thousand.

That is the theory. In practice the sharing is not free, and the price is paid unevenly across endpoints. Worse, the way these models are usually reported hides exactly who paid.

The label matrix is block-sparse, not randomly sparse

The first thing that surprised me is structural rather than algorithmic.

Multitask molecular datasets are sparse — very few compounds carry labels for every endpoint. That much is expected, and masked losses handle it. But the sparsity is not random. Measurements come from assay campaigns, and a campaign measures one property across a chemical series chosen for that programme. The compounds with Caco-2 permeability data are largely not the compounds with hepatotoxicity data.

This matters because co-labelled compounds are precisely where a shared encoder learns that two endpoints are related. A compound measured for both permeability and clearance constrains the representation to explain both at once. A compound measured for one of them constrains nothing about the relationship. When the overlap is concentrated in a few small blocks, most of what the model learns about each endpoint is learned in isolation, and the “shared” representation is shared in name more than in evidence.

So before reaching for a weighting scheme, it is worth measuring the overlap: for each pair of endpoints, how many compounds carry both labels. In my experience that number is often small enough to explain a disappointing result on its own.

Gradients that pull in opposite directions

The algorithmic problem is better known. With shared parameters \(\theta\) and per-task losses \(\mathcal{L}_i\), the update follows the sum \(\sum_i w_i g_i\) where \(g_i = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_i\). Two tasks conflict when their gradients point apart — the condition in Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning is simply \(\cos\varphi_{ij} < 0\).

That paper’s useful contribution, to me, is not the method but the diagnosis. It argues that conflict alone is not what damages training; harm requires three things together, which they call the tragic triad: gradients that conflict, gradients of very different magnitude so one dominates the average, and high curvature along those directions, which makes the dominant task’s gain look larger than it is and the other task’s loss look smaller. All three conditions are easy to satisfy in an ADMET panel, where endpoints differ in data volume by two orders of magnitude.

Their remedy is to project away the conflicting component before summing: when \(g_i \cdot g_j < 0\), replace \(g_i\) with

\[g_i - \frac{g_i \cdot g_j}{\lVert g_j \rVert^2}\, g_j\]

and leave non-conflicting gradients alone. It is cheap, and it is a reasonable default. But it treats a symptom. If two endpoints genuinely demand different representations, removing the conflict from the update does not make them compatible — it just stops one from overwriting the other.

Losses that are not on the same scale

A separate problem gets confused with the first. A squared-error loss on log Papp and a cross-entropy loss on a binary toxicity label produce gradients of quite different magnitude, and the ratio has nothing to do with which endpoint matters. Hand-tuning per-task weights for dozens of endpoints is not a serious option.

The standard answer is to learn the weights as observation noise. Kendall, Gal and Cipolla treat each task’s homoscedastic uncertainty \(\sigma_i\) as a parameter, giving, for a regression and a classification head,

\[\mathcal{L} \approx \frac{1}{2\sigma_1^{2}}\mathcal{L}_1 + \frac{1}{\sigma_2^{2}}\mathcal{L}_2 + \log\sigma_1 + \log\sigma_2\]

A noisy endpoint learns a large \(\sigma\) and is down-weighted; the \(\log\sigma\) terms stop \(\sigma\) from growing without bound, which would otherwise let the model ignore the data entirely. In practice you predict \(s = \log\sigma^2\) for numerical stability.

I like this because the weighting is estimated rather than asserted, and because \(\sigma\) is interpretable after training — an endpoint whose learned noise is high is telling you something about its data.

A third imbalance is easy to miss: sampling. If batches are drawn in proportion to dataset size, a forty-thousand-label endpoint dominates a four-hundred-label one regardless of loss weighting. Temperature sampling, \(p_i \propto n_i^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha < 1\), borrowed from multilingual translation, flattens this.

The measurement problem

Here is the part I think matters most, and it is not a modelling question.

Negative transfer is defined relative to a single-task baseline. An endpoint has suffered from joint training if the multitask model predicts it worse than a model trained on that endpoint alone. Which means: if you have not trained the single-task baselines, you cannot know whether it happened.

Most multitask results are reported as a mean across endpoints, or as a win against a previously published multitask model. Both can improve while a third of the individual endpoints regress. And the regressions are not randomly distributed — the endpoints most likely to be overwritten are the sparse ones with few co-labelled compounds, which are exactly the endpoints the multitask approach was supposed to rescue. An average driven by the data-rich endpoints is not just an incomplete summary; for this purpose it is close to the wrong statistic.

So the honest protocol costs more: train every endpoint alone, train them jointly, and report the per-endpoint difference. The mean can be a summary line, but the table of deltas is the result.

Which endpoints should share a model at all

The obvious next question is whether to group endpoints rather than pool all of them, and the honest answer is that nobody can predict the groups well.

Standley and colleagues studied this directly and found something I keep returning to: the affinity between tasks measured by transfer — how well a representation learned for one task serves another — showed no correlation with how well those tasks actually trained together, Pearson’s \(r = -0.12\), \(p = 0.74\) in their main setting. Relatedness in the intuitive sense is not a reliable predictor of whether joint training helps.

That is an uncomfortable result, because it means the grouping has to be measured rather than reasoned about, and measuring pairwise interactions across dozens of endpoints is quadratic in the number of endpoints. For an ADMET panel that is expensive but not impossible, and it is probably a better use of compute than another architecture search.

Where this leaves me

Multitask learning on ADMET panels is worth doing — I would not have built one otherwise. But I have stopped treating the average as the result. The questions I now ask of any multitask model, including my own:

  • How many compounds carry labels for each pair of endpoints?
  • What is the per-endpoint change against a single-task baseline, not the mean?
  • Which endpoints got worse, and do they share a property — low data volume, a distinct assay, little overlap with the rest?
  • Are the learned \(\sigma\) values telling me something about data quality I should have known beforehand?

None of this is exotic. It is mostly the discipline of comparing against the simpler thing, which is the same lesson I took from comparing molecular representations: the unglamorous baseline is the one that tells you whether the complicated idea earned its place.
entry.summary: Why training many ADMET endpoints in one model is not free, and why the mean across tasks is the wrong thing to report

entry.title: Docking and MD for a viral protein pocket, and what they could not settle

link.title: Docking and MD for a viral protein pocket, and what they could not settle

entry.content:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a leading cause of acute viral hepatitis worldwide, and it hits pregnant women hardest, especially in the third trimester. Why pregnancy makes the infection so much worse has never been fully explained.

Our PNAS study (2026) looks at this through host lipids. It came out of a collaboration between my team at Calici and Professor Scott Kenney’s group at The Ohio State University, together with the Meng laboratory at Virginia Tech. Pregnancy raises circulating free fatty acids, and the paper traces a hormone–lipid–HEV axis: placental lactogen pushes up fatty acid levels in liver and placental cells, oleic acid enhances HEV replication, and blocking phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis reduces it.

Our contribution was the structural modelling: could a fatty acid actually bind the viral protein where the biology suggested it should?

The setup

HEV ORF1 encodes a non-structural polyprotein. An earlier study had predicted a fatty acid–binding domain (FABD) inside its papain-like cysteine protease region, but no one had tested whether fatty acids bind there, or which ones.

We started from the published crystal structure of the HEV zinc-binding non-structural protein (PDB 6NU9) and ran the modelling on Calici’s Pharmaco-Net platform. The pocket was located with the PocketFinder module, then docked with AI-Dock using a 0.2 Å grid and 500 runs per ligand, with binding affinities estimated by the DeepCalici-Plus module.

The ligand set was chosen by the biology, not by convenience. Oleic, linoleic, palmitic and heptadecanoic acids were all raised during placental lactogen treatment or HEV infection in the lipidomics. Mycolipenic acid and a lactone that went down under the same conditions went in as comparisons.

The docking poses then went into molecular dynamics: Amber FF99SB for the protein and GAFF for the ligands, solvated in TIP3P water with an 8 Å buffer and neutralising ions, run in GROMACS 2021.4 through heating, NPT equilibration and a 10 ns production run. Binding free energies came from MM/PBSA on those trajectories.

What we found

The fatty acids fit the pocket; the comparison compounds did not. Oleic, linoleic, palmitic and heptadecanoic acid all docked favourably, between −5.38 and −5.89 kcal/mol. Mycolipenic acid, a branched fatty acid that was downregulated in the lipidomics, gave a positive docking energy, as did the lactone. That the ligand set separated along the same line as the lipidomics was the first sign the pocket was worth taking seriously.

The contact residues held up against evolution. Oleic acid was predicted to hydrogen bond with Ser168 and Glu158 (S683 and E673 in full-length ORF1 numbering), while linoleic and palmitic acid contacted Gly159 and Leu161 instead. We then checked those residues against sequence alignments, which is evidence the docking had no access to. S683 and E673 are conserved across all four human-infecting genotypes, whose FABD regions share 50.6% identity, and absent in Avihepevirus magniiecur, where AlphaFold 3 predicts no FABD structure at all. Residues picked out by a scoring function have no reason to be conserved exactly where the domain exists and missing where it does not.

Affinity is not function. The four fatty acids scored within 0.44 kcal/mol of each other, and MM/PBSA returned large negative binding free energies for all of them, consistent with complexes that stayed associated across the trajectories. When the wet-lab team supplemented infected cells, though, the three tested behaved differently: oleic acid increased HEV replication, palmitic acid reduced it, and linoleic acid did nothing on its own.

Those two observations are not in conflict, and the narrow spread is what I would expect. These are C16 to C18 acyl chains differing by a double bond or two carbons; a scoring function that spread near-identical ligands widely would be the one to distrust. Two ligands can occupy the same site with similar affinity and still do opposite things to the protein, which is the agonist and antagonist problem moved from a receptor into a pocket. Docking asks whether a ligand fits the site and MD asks whether the complex holds together. Neither asks what the protein does next, and the paper speculates that different chains in the pocket may shift the conformation of the protease domain in different directions.

So the modelling turned a domain that had only been predicted from sequence into a specific, testable hypothesis: this pocket, these residues, this class of ligand. What it cannot do on its own is prove that binding there is what drives replication. The paper says so plainly, and the next step it calls for is mutagenesis of the lipid-interacting residues, which are the ones this analysis identified.

What I take from it

Two things stayed with me.

First, the value of the computational part came from how tightly it was tied to the experiments. We treat platform output as a hypothesis, never a result: it has to be checked against bench work, and agreement between the two is the signal we look for. The ligands were chosen from the lipidomics, and the residues it flagged were then checked against sequence conservation across genotypes. On its own, a docking score for one fatty acid in one pocket would have meant very little.

Second, it is worth being precise in print about what a model does and does not establish. The gap between near-identical binding energies and three opposite biological outcomes is the honest result here, and saying so is more useful to the next group than a tidier story would be.

Citation: Yadav KK, Bhandari M, Mahsoub HM, Park YB, Le HV, Choi JM, Brown HM, Rajashekara G, Kenney SP, Meng X-J. Fatty acid regulation and phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis are important for hepatitis E virus replication. PNAS 123(27), e2614150123 (2026). doi:10.1073/pnas.2614150123
entry.summary: Notes on the in silico part of our PNAS study on fatty acids and hepatitis E virus replication

entry.title: What CaliciBoost taught me about molecular representations

link.title: What CaliciBoost taught me about molecular representations

entry.content:
An oral drug has to be absorbed through the intestine before it can work. Caco-2 cell permeability is a widely used in vitro proxy for this intestinal absorption, and predicting it well from structure helps prioritize compounds and saves both time and cost in ADMET screening.

Many models have been built for this task, but most studies focus on a limited set of features or a single modeling approach. In CaliciBoost (Journal of Cheminformatics, 2025), we instead compared a wide range of molecular representations systematically, to see which way of describing a molecule works best for Caco-2 permeability prediction.

The setup

We compared eight molecular representations, from fingerprints to descriptor sets to a learned embedding:

  • Fingerprints: Morgan, Avalon, ErG, MACCS
  • Descriptor sets: RDKit descriptors, PaDEL, Mordred
  • Learned embedding: CDDD

Each representation went through the same pipeline: AutoML training (AutoGluon), feature importance with permutation importance and SHAP, retraining on the top-ranked features, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Using one pipeline for every representation kept the comparison fair.

We used two datasets that differ in scale and chemical diversity. The TDC Caco-2 benchmark has 906 compounds, with the scaffold-based split provided by TDC, so that test molecules have scaffolds not seen in training. We also curated a set of 5,481 compounds from OCHEM, about five times larger. To reduce experimental variability, we excluded measurements labeled basolateral-to-apical, measured at a pH other than 7.4, or measured at a temperature other than 37 °C, and removed duplicates.

What we found

Three things stood out to me.

Descriptor sets did best on the benchmark. On TDC, PaDEL, Mordred and RDKit descriptors gave the lowest errors. The best model, an XGBoost regressor trained on selected PaDEL descriptors, reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.2525 on the test set. Evaluated under the official TDC protocol over five seeds, it scored 0.2560 ± 0.006 and ranked first on the TDC Caco-2 leaderboard. The learned CDDD embedding had the highest error on TDC. Among the most influential PaDEL features were physicochemical and autocorrelation descriptors, such as the number of acidic groups (nAcid) and charge- and mass-weighted autocorrelations.

Feature selection mattered most for the largest descriptor sets. PaDEL provides 1,875 descriptors and Mordred more than 1,800. Trained on all of them, PaDEL (MAE 0.3058) and Mordred (0.3033) trailed RDKit descriptors, Morgan and Avalon. After feature selection and tuning, they moved to the top: the final PaDEL model used its 73 most important features. A smaller, well-chosen subset kept or improved accuracy while making the model easier to interpret.

The dataset changes the ranking. On the larger and more diverse OCHEM set, errors were higher for every representation, and the order shifted: RDKit descriptors did best (MAE 0.3529), while PaDEL fell to fifth. A representation that wins on one benchmark is not guaranteed to win on another, which is a good reason to test on more than one dataset before drawing conclusions.

What I take from it

For me, the main lesson was about where to spend effort. It is tempting to start with the newest architecture, but on a data-limited ADMET task, a careful choice of representation and features, combined with an AutoML model, was enough to reach the top of the benchmark. This is how I now approach other ADMET tasks: compare representations under a fixed pipeline first, then decide whether a more complex model is worth it.

The paper is open access, and the code is on GitHub.

Citation: Le HV, Ren W, Kim J, Yun Y, Park YB, Kim YJ, Han BK, Choi I, Park J-I, Yun H-y, Choi J-M. CaliciBoost: Performance-driven evaluation of molecular representations for Caco-2 permeability prediction. Journal of Cheminformatics 17, 184 (2025). doi:10.1186/s13321-025-01137-7
entry.summary: Notes on our Journal of Cheminformatics paper comparing eight molecular representations for Caco-2 permeability prediction

entry.title: Running Claude Science on Windows, then and now

link.title: Running Claude Science on Windows, then and now

entry.content:
Claude Science is Anthropic’s research application for scientists. It runs locally on your own computer rather than as a website: it sets up its own Python and R environments, connects to scientific databases and tools, and asks before it reads one of your folders or runs code. Results come back as artifacts you can open and download. It needs a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan.

The beta: Linux and macOS only

When I first tried the beta in July 2026, it ran only on macOS and Linux. To make it easier for Windows users to try it, I tested whether the Linux version would run under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL 2). It did, and I shared the steps as a short guide on LinkedIn on 14 July.

Now: a native Windows app

Claude Science now ships a Windows installer. You download it from the product page, open it, and it installs for your user account, adds itself to the Start menu and opens in its own window. No WSL, no terminal. For most Windows users this is the way to go, and it replaces my earlier guide.

A few differences on Windows are worth knowing before you start:

  • Claude runs shell commands with PowerShell. Running git inside cells, Command Prompt scripts and changing folders in PowerShell need a one-time Windows permission. Python and R cells work without it.
  • You can only grant access to folders on local NTFS or ReFS drives, not network shares, mapped drives or most USB sticks.
  • The Model endpoints option under Settings > Compute (NVIDIA BioNeMo NIM) is not available in the Windows app.

When WSL still makes sense

The Linux version under WSL is still documented and supported. I would still pick it if:

  • my pipeline depends on Linux-only command-line tools,
  • I want Model endpoints (BioNeMo NIM), which the Windows app doesn’t offer, or
  • I want the same environment as the Linux servers I run jobs on.

Projects in the two setups are kept separately: work you create under WSL stays in WSL, and the Windows app keeps its own.

A correction to my July guide

My original guide used Ubuntu 22.04. Claude Science’s sandbox now needs bubblewrap 0.8.0 or later, and Ubuntu 22.04 ships an older version, so use Ubuntu 24.04 or newer. The short version of the current WSL setup:

# PowerShell, as Administrator
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

# Inside Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl bubblewrap socat
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install-claude-science.sh | bash
. ~/.profile
claude-science serve --port 8765 --no-browser

Open the printed http://127.0.0.1:8765 link in a Windows browser and sign in. If the link stops working, claude-science url prints a fresh one.

For the official, up-to-date steps, see Get started. My original WSL walkthrough is on LinkedIn; if you follow it, use Ubuntu 24.04 as noted above.
entry.summary: From a WSL workaround during the beta to a native Windows app, and when the Linux route still makes sense
